summary: The paper introduces CODEC, which combines gradient-based attribution (Integrated Gradients applied to hidden units) with sparse autoencoders (SAEs) to decompose per-image hidden-unit contributions into sparse 'modes,' then uses these modes for network control (ablation/preservation) and input-space visualization. Applications span ResNet-50 on ImageNet, a retinal CNN, and a ViT. The framing (SAEs on contributions, not activations) is a useful and reasonable idea, and the perturbation experiments and biological application are appealing. However, the paper is undersold against modern interpretability literature (attribution patching, path patching, ACDC/EAP, sparse feature circuits, transcoders, Anthropic-style SAEs), presents almost no error bars or significance tests on its headline claims, and reports several qualitatively striking results without adequate quantitative baselines, so as-submitted it sits below the ICLR acceptance bar.
strengths: The conceptual move — decompose hidden-unit *contributions* rather than *activations* with an SAE — is a clean and defensible reframing of a hot area, and the layer-wise findings (sparsity increases with depth; positive/negative contributions progressively decorrelate) are non-trivial and interesting.

The perturbation study (ablation and preservation via top mode-weighted channels) provides an actual causal test of whether recovered modes are functionally meaningful, not just correlational, and reports both target-class and off-target curves.

The mode-to-class correlations, and the finding that contribution modes are better class-correlated than activation modes at intermediate layers, gives a concrete metric on which the method beats the natural baseline.

The cross-domain application to a retinal CNN (with the surprisal-based scalar target and dynamic-IRF analysis) is a genuinely interesting biological use case that few pure-interpretability papers attempt.
The paper thinks carefully about the scalar-target design choice (avoiding a 3D per-logit decomposition) and reports basic SAE hyperparameter robustness (threshold, dictionary size, L1, seeds).
Contribution-mapped visualizations (input-space maps restricted to mode channels) are a natural extension of IG that could plausibly be a useful diagnostic tool for practitioners.

key_concerns.issue: Related work and positioning are thin relative to what a 2026 interpretability paper needs. The paper compares SAE-on-contributions almost exclusively to SAE-on-activations and to raw channel analysis. It does not discuss or compare against attribution patching / edge attribution patching, path patching, ACDC/EAP, causal scrubbing, integrated-gradients-based circuit discovery, transcoders / cross-layer SAEs, or recent 'sparse feature circuits' work — all of which target the same problem (causal, sparse, mode-level explanations of network computation).
key_concerns.suggested_fix: Add a dedicated related-work section that names and contrasts these methods, and add at least one head-to-head comparison (e.g., mode-based ablation vs. attribution-patching-selected edges/nodes) on the ImageNet task.

key_concerns.issue: Statistical soundness is weak for a conference paper making quantitative comparative claims. Most reported gains (mode-vs-activation ablation area, mode-vs-channel class correlation, dimensionality/sparsity trends across layers) appear to be single-point estimates with no seed variance, no confidence intervals, and no significance tests. R^2 = 0.85 vs 0.84 is invoked without variance. The SAE hyperparameter sweep is described qualitatively without curves and numeric ranges in the main text.
key_concerns.suggested_fix: Retrain the SAE with multiple seeds per layer, report mean ± std for every headline comparison (mode/channel/activation), and add paired significance tests (or bootstrap CIs) on ablation-area and mode-class correlation across the 1000 classes.

key_concerns.issue: Novelty is real but modest and is somewhat overclaimed. The abstract and body assert that CODEC reveals 'causal processes that cannot be determined by analyzing activations alone' — but IG-style contributions are still a function of the same forward pass and gradient, and the SAE step is standard; the causal-vs-correlational framing is a stronger claim than the reported evidence (correlational mode-class alignment plus channel ablations) supports on its own.
key_concerns.suggested_fix: Reframe claims as 'output-directed decomposition' rather than a categorical causal advantage over activations, and add a controlled test (e.g., activation patching or interchange interventions on the mode-selected channels vs. matched activation-selected channels) to substantiate the causal-strength claim.

key_concerns.issue: The ViT experiment is a single paragraph and the paper explicitly notes 'ablation performance was inferior to that observed in CNNs' without quantifying it, without probing why (spatial reduction over tokens, residual stream mixing, attention-layer contribution definition), and without a fair baseline. As presented it is a negative-ish result that also weakens the generality claims in the abstract.
key_concerns.suggested_fix: Either move ViT to a dedicated section with numbers, alternative spatial-reduction schemes, and a proper baseline (SAE on residual stream / transcoder), or scope the abstract/intro to CNNs and biological models.

key_concerns.issue: Baselines for the perturbation experiment are underspecified. 'Activation modes' and 'random class' are used as comparators, but there is no comparison against strong non-SAE baselines: e.g., ranking channels by mean |contribution|, by IG magnitude directly, by TCAV, by gradient×activation, or by attribution patching. Without those, it is unclear whether the SAE decomposition helps beyond simply using the underlying contribution values directly.
key_concerns.suggested_fix: Add ablation/preservation curves for at least (a) top channels by summed |IG| without SAE, (b) top channels by activation magnitude, (c) attribution-patching-selected channels, on the same target classes.

key_concerns.issue: Calibration issues: the input-visualization results (Fig. 7) are shown for cherry-picked classes without a quantitative interpretability metric; 'shiny wood, hands, etc.' is anecdotal. Similarly, 'sharp increase in ablation efficacy...between blocks 6 and 7' is asserted from a single curve.
key_concerns.suggested_fix: Add a quantitative human or automated evaluation of the input visualizations (e.g., feature-consistency scoring across images) and mark trend claims as suggestive rather than established.

key_concerns.issue: Clarity and structural issues: methodology is scattered across the intro, method, and results; the SAE loss/architecture, threshold semantics, and how 'contribution modes' differ from standard SAE dictionaries are re-derived multiple times. The manuscript is dense and would benefit from an explicit Method section and a self-contained algorithm box.
key_concerns.suggested_fix: Consolidate the method (target, contribution algorithm, SAE definition, mode-selection procedure, perturbation protocol) into one section with an algorithm block, and move exposition currently in results back into method.

key_concerns.issue: Reproducibility, judging only from the described methodology, is adequate but not strong: exact dataset splits are given (ImageNet val 50k), SAE hyperparameters are given, and IG settings (10 steps, top-logit) are specified, but the retinal model dataset, cell counts, train/eval split, and ViT variant hyperparameters are described only in passing, and per-layer expansion factors and thresholds beyond the 'baseline' are not fully tabulated.
key_concerns.suggested_fix: Add a reproducibility table summarizing, per experiment, model, dataset, contribution algorithm and settings, SAE hyperparameters, evaluation metric, and number of seeds.

questions_for_authors: How does CODEC compare quantitatively to attribution patching / EAP / path patching / ACDC and to SAE feature circuits for identifying causally-necessary channels on the same ImageNet target-class ablation task?

Report seed variance: across independent SAE trainings (varying only the seed), how stable are (a) the top mode per class, (b) the ablation-area score in Fig. 6E, and (c) the layerwise dimensionality curve in Fig. 3F?

Baseline: how does 'top-k channels ranked by summed |IG|' (no SAE at all) perform on the ablation/preservation curves relative to CODEC-selected channels? This isolates the value of the SAE step from the value of using contributions.

For the causal claim: have you tested interchange or activation patching on the CODEC-selected channels versus activation-selected channels to directly verify that CODEC identifies more causally-necessary units, rather than just channels whose ablation happens to hurt accuracy more?
For ViT: quantify the 'inferior' ablation performance versus CNNs and versus a residual-stream SAE / transcoder baseline. What specifically about token-as-space reduction is failing?

The claim that positive and negative contributions decorrelate across depth is interesting — is this robust to the choice of contribution algorithm (IG steps, SmoothGrad, ActGrad), and does it hold in networks trained without ReLU (e.g., GELU-based ViTs) once contributions are computed appropriately?
How sensitive are the retinal-CNN mode-cluster results to the choice of surprisal as the scalar target, and what would change with per-cell targets aggregated differently?
calibration_check: Claims are directionally reasonable but overreach in places: statements that contributions reveal 'causal processes that cannot be determined by analyzing activations alone' and broad generality claims (LLMs, ViTs) exceed what the reported experiments — mostly ResNet-50 with correlational mode-class analysis plus channel ablations — actually support.

significance.justification: A useful reframing of SAE-based interpretability toward output-directed decomposition, with a plausible bridge to biological analysis; interesting to the interpretability subfield but not yet a paradigm shift.

novelty.justification: Genuinely new as a combination — IG-style hidden-unit contributions decomposed by an SAE with a scalar target — but each ingredient is standard, and closely related lines (feature circuits, attribution patching, transcoders) already occupy nearby territory.

rigor.justification: The method is defined coherently and the perturbation protocol is sensible, but several causal-strength claims outrun the evidence and key baselines are missing.

statistical_soundness.justification: Headline quantitative comparisons (ablation areas, mode-class correlations, dimensionality/sparsity trends, R^2 gaps) are presented without seed variance, confidence intervals, or significance tests, which is below the ICLR bar for comparative claims.

calibration_honesty.justification: Limitations paragraph is honest about scope, but the abstract/intro overclaim causal superiority over activations and generality to LLMs/ViTs beyond what the experiments show; ViT weaknesses are noted only qualitatively.

clarity.justification: The core idea comes through, but method components are redistributed across sections, notation is dense, and several core definitions (mode, loading, threshold semantics) are stated multiple times without a consolidated method block.

structure_compliance.justification: Standard conference structure is roughly present (abstract, motivation, method-in-results, experiments, biological application, ViT, limitations), but there is no dedicated Method or Related Work section; length is within ICLR norms.

reproducibility.justification: Judging only from described methodology, standard datasets and IG/SAE hyperparameters are specified enough that a diligent reader could re-implement the ImageNet pipeline; retinal and ViT settings are less complete, and seed/variance information is thin.

related_work.justification: Positioning against modern causal-interpretability and SAE literature (attribution patching, path patching, ACDC/EAP, sparse feature circuits, transcoders, Anthropic-style SAEs) is largely missing in the prose, which weakens the contribution's delineation independent of any missing reference list.

figure_quality.justification: From the captions, the figures are targeted and support the specific quantitative claims (sparsity, decorrelation, mode-class correlation, ablation curves, dynamic IRFs), though several rely on hand-picked example classes.

breadth_generality.justification: Coverage spans a CNN, a retinal model, and a ViT, which is broader than typical, but the ViT experiment is preliminary and negative-leaning, and the LLM claim in the abstract is not backed by main-text experiments, so the generality claim is under-supported.

overall_recommendation.justification: Borderline reject: an interesting, well-motivated idea with promising CNN and retinal results, but insufficient statistical rigor, missing modern causal-interpretability baselines, and overreaching claims put it below the ICLR acceptance bar as submitted.
